feedback: If a child names a face by the solid's name (calls a cylinder's end 'a cylinder'), trace round or stamp that face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is the 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder.
If a child calls a cube 'a square', pop up or unfold the six square faces so they see the solid is made OF squares, then help them re-name the solid.
If a child treats the solid as one undifferentiated whole, unfold it so each face lies flat and gets named, then rebuild it face by face.

Note for the teacher: a paper or card face has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat (zero-thickness) 2-D shape of the solid's face; ask the child what mathematical shape the flattened face represents, treating the paper as a stand-in rather than the mathematical shape itself.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid's flat faces are 2-D shapes; a solid with only flat faces (such as a cube or pyramid) is built from them, while a cylinder also has a curved surface. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether it is drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.
learnerActions: Handle a real solid (a tin/cylinder, a cube, a square-based pyramid) and run a finger over its surfaces.
Unfold or 'pop up' a solid made from flat paper/card so its faces lie flat, then touch and count the separated faces.

Name each flattened face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) and rebuild the solid face by face. If a paper cylinder is unrolled, its curved side flattens into a rectangle, but on the cylinder that part is the curved surface, not a flat face.
State the link aloud: 'a cube is made of six squares', 'a cylinder has two circular faces and a curved surface'.
activities.title: Take a solid apart into its flat faces

feedback: When the stamped circle appears beside the tin, confirm: 'the flat end is a circle; the whole tin is the cylinder'.
If a child tries to stamp the curved side, notice it cannot print a single flat shape — only flat faces rest flat and print cleanly.
Note for the teacher: the printed mark (and the paper it is on) has slight thickness; it represents the ideal flat 2-D shape of the solid's face, which is the shape the child names.
activities.intendedInsight: The print of a solid's flat face is a plain 2-D shape (a tin's end prints a circle), making concrete that the face is itself a 2-D shape.
learnerActions: Dip the flat end of a tin in paint (or ink pad) and stamp it on paper; name the shape that appears.
Trace round a flat face of a cube or the square base of a pyramid and name the printed 2-D shape.
Set the printed 2-D shape beside the solid and say which face of the solid it came from.
activities.title: Print the face: trace and paint-stamp

feedback: If a child calls the cylinder's curved side a face, have them try to make it rest flat — it rolls, so it is a curved surface, not a flat face.
Confirm the cylinder has exactly two flat circular faces plus one curved surface.
activities.intendedInsight: A flat face rests flat and has a 2-D shape; a curved surface rolls and is not a flat face — so a cylinder's curved side should not be counted as a flat face.
learnerActions: Try to rest each surface of a cylinder flat on the table: the two ends sit flat, the curved side rolls.
Sort surfaces into 'flat faces' (rest flat) and 'curved surfaces' (roll).
Count and name the flat faces on a cube, a square-based pyramid, and the cylinder; note the cylinder's side is curved, not a flat face.
activities.title: Flat faces versus curved surfaces
